name: Macimorelin
lead: Macimorelin (brand name Macrilen) is an orally active ghrelin-receptor agonist that stimulates release of growth hormone. It is approved by the US FDA as a diagnostic test for adult growth hormone deficiency (AGHD), not as a treatment.[1][2]

In the test, a single oral dose is given and growth hormone levels are measured afterwards. Trials compared it with the insulin tolerance test and with arginine plus GHRH testing.[3][4][5] The US label lists QT prolongation among its warnings.[2]

No studies have tested macimorelin for appearance or muscle-building purposes in healthy people. It appears in looksmaxxing-adjacent discussion as one of the ghrelin-mimetic growth hormone secretagogues, the class that also includes research compounds discussed for GH and IGF-1 raising.
infobox: Aeterna Zentaris; rights held by Novo Nordisk 2018-2022[1]
C26H30N6O3, about 474.6 g/mol; codes AEZS-130, JMV 1843[1]

paras: The US label indicates macrilen for the diagnosis of adult growth hormone deficiency. Its safety and diagnostic performance have not been established in people with a body mass index above 40.[2] Wikipedia describes it as the first oral test of its kind, as other stimulation tests such as the insulin tolerance test are given by injection and the insulin tolerance test can cause severe hypoglycemia.[1][3]

Adult GH deficiency is hard to diagnose because GH is released in pulses, so random blood measurements are not recommended for screening and one or more stimulation tests may be needed.[15] A review of adult diagnosis describes the condition as associated with increased visceral adiposity, decreased lean body mass and bone density, and impaired quality of life, and advises testing only patients at risk for pituitary dysfunction, such as after pituitary surgery, radiation or traumatic brain injury.[10] Because the insulin tolerance test, long the reference standard, is labour-intensive and can cause severe hypoglycemia, an oral alternative was developed.[3][4]

Macimorelin activates growth hormone secretagogue receptors in the pituitary and hypothalamus, triggering growth hormone release.[2] In healthy volunteers it also affected other pituitary hormones, including copeptin and oxytocin, in small studies.[6][7]
The drug is metabolised mainly by CYP3A4 in the liver; the label cautions that strong CYP3A4 inducers can cause false-positive results.[1][2]

The most common reactions listed on the US label include altered taste, dizziness, headache, fatigue, nausea, hunger, diarrhea and upper respiratory infection.[2] The label warns of QT-interval prolongation of about 11 msec and advises avoiding other QT-prolonging drugs.[2] No pregnancy data are available, but use is single-dose.[2]
A thorough QT study in healthy participants and a single-dose safety and pharmacokinetics study in healthy adults underpin the label's cardiac and tolerability statements.[13][17]
No studies found in healthy people for appearance outcomes. Human research is on diagnosis, safety and one small supportive-care pilot.

Diagnostic work: A multicentre open-label study validated macimorelin against arginine plus GHRH testing for adult GH deficiency.[3] A later multicentre phase 3 randomised study compared it with the insulin tolerance test, which the investigators describe as labour-intensive, capable of causing severe hypoglycemia and contraindicated for some patients,[4] and a registered 157-person validation trial (started December 2015) also assessed performance.[16] Further analyses reported its sensitivity and specificity.[5] A paediatric phase 3 study in 101 children was registered from November 2021.[8]

Safety: Phase 1 work in healthy adults examined tolerability, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics after a single dose,[17] and a thorough QT study evaluated cardiac safety, supporting the label's QT warning.[13] In small studies in healthy volunteers it also affected copeptin and oxytocin.[6][7]

Cachexia pilot: A pilot randomised trial in patients with cancer cachexia gave macimorelin for one week, with 10 patients on drug (0.5 or 1.0 mg/kg) and 5 on placebo; two patients on drug met the weight-gain criterion and none on placebo, with no IGF-1 criterion met in either group, and the authors framed it as a pilot of safety and efficacy.[12][9]

Other research: Laboratory researchers have explored the ghrelin receptor agonist for seizure suppression in pharmacoresistant epilepsy models,[14] and a Growth Hormone Research Society Delphi survey mapped clinicians' consensus and disagreements on diagnosing GH deficiency.[11] One review noted that macimorelin did not provide a sufficient stimulus in testing for arginine vasopressin deficiency, a different diagnostic question.[10]

Macimorelin (also coded AEZS-130 and JMV 1843) was invented and first synthesised at the University of Montpellier and CNRS in France in a long-running collaboration with Aeterna Zentaris, which in-licensed it and carried out development.[1] Phase 3 testing was under way by January 2014, when the FDA accepted the new drug application for filing, and the FDA approved it as the first oral test of its kind in December 2017.[1] Novo Nordisk bought the rights in November 2018 for 145 million US dollars and returned them to Aeterna Zentaris in 2022.[1]
In the EU it is prescription-only and the EMA lists it under the later name Ghryvelin.[1]

timeline.event: Validation study of the oral macimorelin test for adult GH deficiency is published.[3]

card.summary: Oral ghrelin-receptor agonist approved only as a one-time diagnostic for adult GH deficiency; nothing on looks.
card.note: Approved only as a diagnostic test; label warns of QT prolongation.

quick.overview:
Macimorelin is a prescription drug sold as Macrilen. Doctors give it once, by mouth, to see whether the pituitary releases enough growth hormone, which helps diagnose adult growth hormone deficiency.

It was approved in the US in December 2017. It is not approved as a treatment and no study has tested it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: It binds the ghrelin (GH secretagogue) receptor in the pituitary and hypothalamus, which prompts a pulse of growth hormone that can be measured.
quick.risks: The label lists altered taste, dizziness, headache and nausea as common reactions and warns of QT prolongation. Strong CYP3A4 inducers can distort test results.

chain: A single oral dose tests whether the pituitary releases growth hormone
A confirmed deficiency opens the way to physician-supervised GH replacement
Replacement addresses the deficiency's link to higher visceral fat and lower lean mass
angle.text: Macimorelin is a diagnostic, not a physique product. Its link to appearance runs through diagnosis: adult GH deficiency is associated with more visceral fat and less lean body mass, and a clear diagnosis is what allows clinicians to decide on replacement.[10]
